Q27966298.summary: Seven arched niches, separated by slender columns with simple Corinthian capitals, run along this sarcophagus front. In the central niche stands a youthful, beardless Christ wearing the toga, his right hand at his breast and a scroll in his left; Peter and Paul turn toward him from the neighbouring niches, and pairs of apostles converse on either side, one of them taking a scroll from a book-box at his feet. The museum reads the central group as a variant of the Roman 'Traditio Legis', Christ giving the new Law to his apostles.
facts: The museum notes that the corner reinforcements left inside the chest when it was hollowed out are characteristic of the sarcophagi of southwestern France.
Its left short side shows Abraham about to sacrifice Isaac, a scene read by early Christians as a type of Christ's sacrifice and of salvation.
According to the museum's record it was reused in the Middle Ages to frame a church portal, so the place of its first use is unknown.
Q27966298.notes: POP: '4e quart 4e siècle ; 5e siècle'. The record names Saint-Michel-du-Touch (Toulouse) as findspot; the precise church where it was reused is only partly legible in the record as fetched. Identification of Peter and Paul follows the museum.

cur:monumental-smm-aphrodisius.summary: Outside the walled Egyptian city of Sotinen, the governor Aphrodisius, followed by his philosophers and soldiers, comes out to greet the Holy Family; the young Christ, haloed and dressed in gold, stands at the centre between Mary and Joseph, accompanied by angels. The episode is drawn from apocryphal infancy legends, in which the idols of Egypt fall before the child and the governor acknowledges him as Lord. It is a rare monumental image of this story and a striking statement of Christ's sovereignty over the pagan world.
cur:monumental-smm-aphrodisius.scripture: Matthew 2:13–15 (with the apocryphal Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew 22–24)
facts: The triumphal-arch mosaics were made under Pope Sixtus III (432–440), whose dedication SIXTUS EPISCOPUS PLEBI DEI ('Sixtus the bishop to the people of God') is inscribed on the arch.
The story of Aphrodisius is told in the apocryphal Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, not in the canonical Gospels.

cur:monumental2-banganarti-descent-into-.summary: On a dark grey ground at the left, a large haloed figure – its paint largely lost, so that it survives mainly as a pale silhouette – reaches down to a tangle of small naked figures rising from the depths, the souls of the dead freed from Hades. At the right, against a glowing orange ground, a smaller standing figure in a pale robe completes the composition above a band of interlace.
facts: Banganarti, near Old Dongola, the capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, was excavated by Polish archaeologists, who recovered a large body of wall paintings from its churches.
cur:monumental2-banganarti-descent-into-.notes: Identification and date follow the photographer's Commons description ('Harrowing of Hell, turn of 11th cent., today in Poznań'). Christ's figure is largely effaced; the identification is consistent with the composition but could not be confirmed from a museum record.

cur:objects-ravenna-carolingian-christ-m.summary: Within a beaded roundel set in a frame of lush acanthus, Christ appears in half-length with a cross-nimbus, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a closed book against his chest. His calm, frontal face and the simple folds of his mantle give the small plaque the gravity of an icon. It belongs to the revival of Late Antique forms under Charlemagne, when ivory carvers again presented Christ as the teacher and Lord of the Gospel.
facts: The museum groups this plaque with a companion plaque showing the angel, symbol of St Matthew, both attributed to Carolingian North Italy around 790–810.
Such square plaques were typically set into the jewelled or carved covers of gospel books, where Christ was often surrounded by the evangelists' symbols (type).

cur:objects-worcester-koimesis-ivory.summary: Within a frame of carved ornament the Virgin lies on her bier, mourned by the apostles who bend toward her from both sides. Behind the bier stands Christ, holding the little swaddled figure of her soul, while angels fly in from the upper corners. The horizontal format allows the mourners to unfold in a quiet, rhythmic procession around the central figure of the Lord.
facts: In the Koimesis, Christ receiving his Mother's soul is the visual centre of the composition; the image became one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine year (tradition).

Q974674.summary: Above the humble stable where Mary kneels before the Christ Child, twelve angels dance in a ring beneath a golden dome of heaven, while below angels embrace men and little devils flee into cracks in the earth. Painted in the troubled Florence that followed the preaching and execution of Savonarola, it is an ecstatic, visionary image of the Nativity as the beginning of the world's final peace. It is quite unlike anything else in Botticelli's work.
facts: It is Botticelli's only signed work, dated 1500 in a cryptic Greek inscription that speaks of 'the troubles of Italy' and of the Apocalypse.
The archaic, varying scale of the figures — Mary is far larger than the shepherds — is a deliberate return to medieval devotional conventions.
Its patron is unknown; the painting may have been made for private devotion, perhaps for a follower of Savonarola.
